A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sparse-PCA work. Their complete main text, equations, algorithms, six figures, references, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic experiments, sample-splitting and scaling ablations, and analysis of NYTimes bag-of-words data, illustrated in Figures 1–6.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the original synthetic experiments, ablations, and NYTimes data analysis, including their reported outcomes in Figures 1–6.

M1.justification: RTPM, its full-sample and disjoint-sample variants, and the deflation procedure are unchanged. Sample splitting, basis-vector restarts, truncation, and Rayleigh-quotient selection retain the same definitions.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same spiked-covariance and counterexample-based synthetic scenarios and the same NYTimes bag-of-words application. No datasets or task scenarios are added or removed.

E2.justification: Figures 2–3 retain DiagThresh, CovThresh, GreedyCorr, and the FPS/ADMM SDP approach from [VCLR13] in their corresponding comparisons. Figure 1 retains RTPM-full versus RTPM-disjoint. The additional [WLL14] citation concerns theoretical runtime, not a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Section 5 retains its metrics, sample sizes, covariance constructions, preprocessing, and iteration/truncation settings. For example, scaling experiments still use d = 2500, r = 10s, and T = 100; NYTimes still uses 10,000 documents and 20,000 features.

E4.justification: The sample-splitting ablation, heuristic-counterexample experiments, scaling analyses, and real-data case study are unchanged. No additional robustness tests or supplementary analyses appear in the appendices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, random-seed details, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The plotted reporting conventions and scaling-curve fitting procedures are unchanged.

E6.justification: Figures 1–6 retain the same empirical curves, points, component weights, and word rankings. Section 5 reports the same performance and qualitative findings. The revised asymptotic runtime comparison is not a change in measured performance.

T1.justification: Section 1.1 revises the theoretical runtime-advantage comparison from Ω(d^2.5) to Ω(d^2), explicitly referencing [WLL14]. This is a localized complexity correction; RTPM's O(nd^2) runtime bound, convergence theorems, counterexamples, and proofs in Appendices A–B are unchanged.

C1.justification: The claimed speedup over SDP-based methods in Section 1.1 is narrowed from Ω(d^2.5) to Ω(d^2). The central contributions—general-covariance recovery, counterexamples to existing heuristics, and recovery of a vector in a sparse leading eigenspace—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 1.2 newly acknowledges that some Model 1 algorithms, including diagonal thresholding, can run in O(d·poly(s log(d))) time, and identifies achieving similar runtime under Model 2 as open. This adds a specific qualification to the paper's efficiency positioning.

D1.justification: Implementation descriptions, experimental hyperparameters, preprocessing, and data-access information are unchanged. The expanded funding and personal acknowledgments add no technical reproducibility information.

R1.justification: The runtime comparison now explicitly cites the already-referenced [WLL14], and Section 1.2 adds the distinction between linear-in-d spiked-model algorithms and the unresolved general-model runtime target. The bibliography itself is unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes consist of a localized contribution-statement edit, a short related-work paragraph, expanded acknowledgments, and revision metadata. The overall section organization and most prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Added text causes local page reflow, including moving Algorithm 4 from PDF page 12 to page 13 and changing its placement relative to Lemma 4. Figures 1–6 retain their plots, captions, axes, and legends.

improvement.justification: The reduced runtime-advantage claim and explicit [WLL14] attribution make the contribution comparison more restrained and specific. The new discussion of linear-in-d algorithms clarifies an unresolved efficiency limitation. These are useful improvements in scientific positioning, while the method, formal recovery guarantees, empirical evidence, and appendices remain unchanged.
